newsitem.title: CONGO: Moves to end Brazzaville showdown intensify.
newsitem.headline: Moves to end Brazzaville showdown intensify.

text.p: Mediation efforts to end a showdown between Congo's President Pascal Lissouba and former Marxist military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso gather pace this weekend after over a week of political and ethnic bloodshed.

About an hour of sustained fighting with automatic weapons and mortar bombs or rocket-propelled grenades broke out around Brazzaville international airport after nightfall on Friday and there were reports of shooting elsewhere.
A semblance of normality had earlier returned to the capital of the former French colony, with some residents emerging from their homes to exchange greetings and condolences.

Aides to Brazzaville mayor Bernard Kolelas said a mediation committee he heads had won agreement from Lissouba and Sassou Nguesso to meet for peace talks in Gabon with its veteran president, Omar Bongo, acting as host and chief mediator.

"The meeting will probably take place on Sunday because tomorrow representatives of Lissouba and Sassou will meet with the mediating committee which will discuss the points which will be on the agenda at the negotiations," Kolelas spokesman Hellot Mampouya told Reuters on Friday.
A Lissouba spokesman said he had heard of the proposed meeting but could not confirm Lissouba would attend. Neither Sassou Nguesso nor a spokesman was immediately available for comment.
Mohamed Sahnoun, the special U.N. and Organisation of African Unity envoy to the region, told Reuters in Kinshasa that he was in touch with Bongo and all sides in the conflict.

Bodies still littered Brazzaville's streets on Friday. Aid workers and military officials had not been able to reach all areas to compile a reliable death toll, which some sources say could run into hundreds and maybe even several thousand.
The conflict erupted on June 5 after the army surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home as part of a crackdown on private militias and unauthorised arms in the runup to a July 27 election.
Sassou Nguesso's Cobra militia retaliated, pushing back Lissouba supporters in the armed forces in some places.

After disputed parliamentary elections in 1993, supporters of Kolelas, runner-up to Lissouba in a 1992 presidential election, were in the thick of fighting which killed at least 2,000 people. This time they stayed out of the conflict.
Lissouba and Sassou Nguesso told their forces to cease fire on Wednesday, but sporadic clashes continued.
"It might be early to be certain but it (the ceasefire) seems to be taking hold," Bertin Mulunga, another Kolelas aide, said on Friday.

France said in Paris that it would start pulling its troops out of Brazzaville on Sunday. French troops have evacuated 4,300 foreign nationals, including 1,550 French citizens. The government did not say how long the withdrawal would take.
"Our mission is essentially accomplished but it's possible that there could be some evacuations tomorrow," French army spokesman Henry Pelissier said in Brazzaville on Friday.

Edmond Munungi, another Kolelas aide, said the mediation committee agreed a peace blueprint envisaging the assembly of fighters and mixed patrols. "Both sides have representatives on the committee so we hope this will be respected," he said.
Sassou Nguesso, named president in 1979, bowed to pressure for multi-party politics in 1990 but was among candidates knocked out in the first round of the 1992 poll.
He returned to Congo in January after over a year in France and launched into an undeclared campaign for the presidency.
